sketches.title: Counterfeit Wisdom
sketches.premise: The Host announces a proverb that sounds ancient but was invented five seconds ago. Turn its two plain nouns into a grand little law of life; the Host decides whether your version still obeys the announced rule. First move: take the opening proverb and make it useful, nasty, or gloriously wrong-headed.
sketches.criterion: The answer must keep the proverb's stated cause-and-effect or advice true in the situation it describes, without merely repeating it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence of advice, warning, or commentary that applies the fake proverb to a new situation, under 90 characters; example: Card: "A warm spoon forgives no soup." Move: "Never trust the smiling waiter with your emergency chili."
sketches.first_card: A lonely shoe remembers every puddle.

sketches.title: Ancient Meaning
sketches.premise: A fake proverb arrives wearing a dusty beard and pretending to explain the world. Give it a concrete scene that makes its strange wisdom look true, while the Host clinically tests whether both key nouns still matter. The best answer sounds like a proverb just discovered in a cracked temple wall.
sketches.criterion: The answer must show a believable situation in which the proverb's relationship between its two nouns remains true.
sketches.move_shape: Write a vivid mini-scene, caption, or example under 90 characters; example: Card: "A locked sandwich fears the moon." Move: "At midnight, the sealed lunchbox stayed shut beneath the window."
sketches.first_card: A borrowed ladder insults the sky.

sketches.title: Ritual of Two
sketches.premise: Each fake proverb names two ordinary things, and the Host orders a ceremonial pairing. Use both nouns in a tiny ritual, rule, or public announcement that gives the old-sounding line a new job. The Host will praise your ceremony, then dissect it like a frog in a lab.
sketches.criterion: Both nouns must appear and remain in the same meaningful relationship promised by the proverb, rather than serving as decorative name-drops.
sketches.move_shape: Write a ritual instruction or official rule under 90 characters; example: Card: "The quiet fork chooses the loud plate." Move: "At dinner, the quiet fork points to whoever wants seconds."
sketches.first_card: A red sock guides a patient river.

sketches.title: Proverb Trial
sketches.premise: The Host puts a fake proverb on trial for being suspiciously wise. You are the prosecution or defense: give one exhibit, witness line, or verdict that tests the proverb without denying its core claim. Sharp lies are welcome; only the announced wisdom is protected by law.
sketches.criterion: The answer must use the proverb's claim as true evidence or reasoning, even while inventing the trial's people, crime, and verdict.
sketches.move_shape: Write a courtroom line, exhibit label, or verdict under 90 characters; example: Card: "A hungry bell summons no fish." Move: "Exhibit A: three rings, zero trout, and one furious fisherman."
sketches.first_card: A cracked window trusts no winter.

sketches.title: Field Guide to Fakes
sketches.premise: The Host has catalogued a new species of proverb and wants a field-note entry. Describe where it appears, how it behaves, or how to survive it, using the two nouns as if they belong to one strange ecosystem. Clinical accuracy earns points; dramatic nonsense earns more if the species still behaves correctly.
sketches.criterion: The entry must preserve the proverb's real-world rule about how its two nouns act or affect each other.
sketches.move_shape: Write a field-guide note under 90 characters; example: Card: "A polite hammer avoids a crooked nail." Move: "Habitat: rude workshops; warning sign: the nail suddenly stands straight."
sketches.first_card: A sleepy key wakes a stubborn door.

sketches.title: Last-Word Lore
sketches.premise: The Host gives you a fake proverb and a final word to build toward. Write a tiny legend, warning, or punchline that ends on that word while making the proverb sound like the reason anyone remembers it. The Host checks the old wisdom first and your nerve second.
sketches.criterion: The answer must end with the supplied final word and make the proverb's stated relationship remain true.
sketches.move_shape: Write a one- or two-line legend under 90 characters, ending with the card's word; example: Card: "A jealous candle hides from the sun." End word: "ash". Move: "It burned all night to avoid dawn. By sunrise, only ash."
sketches.first_card: A careful spoon survives the hungry mouth. End word: "again"
